final_proof:
Proof. Write ℕ = {0,1,2,…}. We first establish a fact about generalized sums.

Let (t_i)_{i∈I} be a family of nonnegative real numbers which vanishes outside S⊆I. Suppose the net

P_F = ∑_{i∈F} t_i,

indexed by the finite subsets F⊆I ordered by inclusion, converges to L. Let e:S→ℕ be injective, and define

z_n = t_i if n=e(i) for some i∈S, and z_n=0 otherwise.

Then ∑_{n=0}^∞ z_n=L. Indeed, since (P_F) is increasing and converges to L, we have L=sup_F P_F. For N≥0, let

E_N={i∈S:e(i)≤N}.

This is finite, and

∑_{n=0}^N z_n=P_{E_N}≤L.

Thus these partial sums increase to some Q≤L. Conversely, if F⊆I is finite, then P_F=P_{F∩S}. The finite set e(F∩S) is contained in {0,…,N} for some N, so

P_F≤P_{E_N}≤Q.

Taking the supremum over finite F gives L≤Q. Hence Q=L. Notice that the ordinary series here begins at n=0.

For each a∈{1,…,m}, let

S_a={i∈I:x_a(i)≠0},   S=⋃_{a=1}^m S_a.

Every S_a is countable, so the finite union S is countable. Choose an injection e:S→ℕ. For each a define the real sequence y_a=(y_{a,n})_{n≥0} by

y_{a,n}=x_a(i) if n=e(i) for some i∈S, and y_{a,n}=0 if n∉e(S).

This is well-defined because e is injective. Apply the preceding fact to t_i=x_a(i)^2. The corresponding finite-subsum net converges because x_a∈A, and t_i vanishes outside S. Therefore

∑_{n=0}^∞ y_{a,n}^2 = ∑_{i∈I} x_a(i)^2 < ∞.

Thus y_a∈ℓ² for every a.

Now fix a,b∈{1,…,m}. The generalized sum of (x_a(i)−x_b(i))² exists and is finite. Indeed, for every finite F⊆I,

∑_{i∈F}(x_a(i)−x_b(i))²
≤2∑_{i∈F}x_a(i)²+2∑_{i∈F}x_b(i)²
≤2L_a+2L_b,

where L_c=∑_{i∈I}x_c(i)². Hence the net of finite subsums on the left is increasing and bounded above, and therefore converges to its supremum. It also vanishes outside S.

For every n, y_{a,n}−y_{b,n}=x_a(i)−x_b(i) when n=e(i), and it is zero when n∉e(S). Applying the established fact to t_i=(x_a(i)−x_b(i))² gives

∑_{n=0}^∞(y_{a,n}−y_{b,n})²
=∑_{i∈I}(x_a(i)−x_b(i))².

Taking nonnegative square roots yields

d_{ℓ²}(y_a,y_b)=d_2(x_a,x_b).

Finally, equality is preserved in both directions. If x_a=x_b, the construction immediately gives y_a=y_b. Conversely, suppose y_a=y_b. For every i∈S,

x_a(i)=y_{a,e(i)}=y_{b,e(i)}=x_b(i),

and for i∉S both x_a(i) and x_b(i) are zero. Thus x_a=x_b. Consequently,

y_a≠y_b ⇔ x_a≠x_b

for every a,b∈{1,…,m}, while all pairwise distances are preserved, as required. ∎
